notes: West leads the ♠Q against 7NT. South must take 7 club tricks. Normally 10 card suits missing the Queen do not provide much scope in the play. However, the blockage of this suit gives South some options.

South wins the opening lead and leads a club out of his hand. When West follows low, South must decide what to play from dummy. If West has at least 2 clubs including the ♣Q, South must finesse on the first round. When East cannot win this trick running the clubs will be easy.

Playing the ♣K or ♣A on the first round of the suit is essentially playing East for a singleton ♣Q. If the ♣Q is guarded once, South will go down after cashing a top honour. The other top club honour will drop the ♣Q, but the suit will be blocked.
If West has all 3 clubs, South will still go down after cashing a top honour. South can cross back to his hand and play a club. West will cover and the suit will be blocked.
Finessing on the first round of clubs is easily the best play. As the saying goes, 8 ever, 9 never, 10 -- on this deal.

South can make the contract even if all three finesses are wrong by playing for an elimination. South should cash the top diamonds and, when the ♦Q is still out, exit a third round.

If West wins the ♦Q and exits a club (he should have switched to a club at trick 2), South ducks in dummy. East can win, but he will be endplayed. A club return, will pick up the suit for 1 loser. A heart return will yield a ruff and discard.

If West has a diamond to return South can win in hand and pass a club to East, enplaying him as before. If East wins the third round of diamonds, his only safe exit will be in diamonds. South can win that trick and pass a club to East. Once again, East will be endplayed.

notes: West leads the ♣10 against 7NT. After winning the club opening lead, South should unblock the hearts and try 2 rounds of spades.

When West discards on the second round of spades, East must have 4 or more diamonds for the contract to have a chance. South must plan to squeeze East in spades and diamonds. One of the threats will have to be in South's hand for the squeeze to function. As North holds winners in both spades and diamonds and South has no hand entry in either of these suits, South must execute a Vienna coup.
A Vienna coup is an unblocking play to prepare for a squeeze. If South fails to cash North's winners in one of the threat suits, the last round of clubs will squeeze North before East.

Assume dummy's third spade honour is cashed, establishing South's spade as an unblocked threat against East. Dummy's heart winner is cashed for a diamond pitch. East will be squeezed on the run of the clubs.
On the last club, North can spare a spade while East is squeezed. A spade discard will establish South's spade. A diamond discard will make North's third diamond a winner.

South's best plan is to play the ♦K and overtake with North's ♦A. South can pick up East's spades with the aid of the proven finesse. South now tries to get back the diamond trick he previously compressed. He finesses West for the ♦J. As East started with all 3 spades, this finesse is better than even money to succeed. notes: West leads the ♥Q against 6NT. West's heart opening lead is won by South. South must avoid losing a trick to the ♣J in order to come to 12 tricks. The club combination is common and is frequently misplayed.

South should begin by leading a club towards dummy. When West follows low the ♣K or ♣Q should be played from dummy. It is a well-known defensive tactic for East to duck with ♣A doubleton of clubs in this situation in order to leave declarer with a guess on the second round. When the ♣Q holds the first trick, South has no inference as to the position of the ♣A.

South returns to the closed hand and plays a second club. When West follows low it seems that South has a strict guess. Playing a low club will work when East began with doubleton ♣A. Playing the ♣K will work when East began with a doubleton ♣J. The odds of these 2 holdings are the same.

This is actually not a guess. It is correct to play the ♣K on the second round. When a declarer is faced with a problem such as this, he should formulate a plan and not deviate from that plan based on the defenders' early plays in the suit.

If declarer's plan is to play West for the ♣J on the second round of the suit, it is irrelevant whether East wins the ♣A on the first round when holding a doubleton. Declarer will always pick up that holding no matter how East defends.

If declarer's plan is to play West for the ♣A on the second round of the suit, East, holding doubleton ♣A, can always defeat the contract by ducking the first round. If East wins the ♣A on the first round, South should play him for ♣AJ doubleton.

The above club layout should only be picked up if declarer was planning on playing the ♣K on the second round of the suit. This holding makes it correct to play the ♣K on the second round regardless of whether East wins the ♣A or the ♣Q holds on the first round.

East must have the ♠Q as West would have opened the bidding with the ♠Q in addition to the 10 points in clubs and the ♦J he has already shown. If East has the diamond length, he can be squeezed if he has the ♠Q, ♠10, and ♠9 or 5 or more spades.

If West has the diamond length, he can be squeezed if he has the ♠10 and ♠9. In any case, South cashes the remaining top diamonds and runs the hearts. As West has the long diamonds as well as the required spade holding, he will have no good answer on the last heart. A diamond discard will make North's diamond good.

A spade discard will allow South to take 3 spade tricks. The ♠J is led from North (the hand would have played equally well if the ♠J was led earlier). East must cover. South wins and his third spade will be worth a trick.

If East follows with a middle heart (or the ♥Q) on the first round of trump, South should win the ♥A or ♥K. South has plenty of dummy entries to pick up East's trump holding by finessing two more times.

If this is the case, South's best chance is to draw trump ending in the closed hand and play a low club towards the dummy. If the ♣10 is with West and the ♣Q is with East, West must duck. This line of play will look silly if the cards are distributed as above. West will win the ♣Q and play a diamond through dummy. All South had to do was lead clubs towards the ♣K.

This East hand is impossible, however. East is a passed hand. He is marked with the ♥A and ♥Q from the opening lead. If East really has the ♣A he cannot have the ♦K as well or he would have opened the bidding.
Any time that leading a club towards the ♣K works, the diamond finesse will also work. It is thus correct to lead a small club towards the dummy intending to play the ♣9.

notes: West leads the ♦K against 5♠. West cashes 2 diamond tricks and switches to the ♥J won by South. The contract is in serious trouble. West will need a singleton ♠J for the trump suit to be playable for no losers. West's play of the ♥J, apparently denying the ♥Q, gives South hope of not having to lose any heart tricks.

South should cross to the ♣A and lead the ♠Q. When East follows low and West produces the ♠J, prospects have improved. The ♠10 is also ducked by East. South is able to remain in the dummy and play a heart to the ♥10.

Unfortunately West produces the ♥Q. Usually one should not mind paying off to a clever falsecard like West's ♥J switch. In this case, South should have worked it out. If East really had the ♥Q, the ♠10 would have been covered by the ♠K. South would have been locked in the closed hand and would have had no way to avoid giving East a heart trick.
South should not play East to have misdefended in such an easy situation. When the ♠10 is not covered, West should be played for doubleton ♥QJ.

As West has 2 certain trump tricks, South must avoid a heart loser. The only hope is to take 4 club tricks, discarding dummy's ♥2 on the last round. South's heart loser can then be ruffed in dummy.

For this plan to work, West must follow to all 4 rounds of clubs. Since West must have length in clubs, he should be played for the ♣J. South should lead the ♣9 or ♣10 and pass it when West follows low.

If West has the hoped for distribution, there is nothing he can do. South plays 3 more rounds of clubs discarding dummy's ♥2 on the last round. South can now ruff his heart loser in the dummy and concede 2 trump tricks.

notes: West leads the ♣K against 4♠. West wins the first trick and switches to diamonds. South must lose a trick in diamonds. The only possible problem is that 2 trump tricks may have to be lost.
South should duck the diamond shift in an attempt to sever the link between the defenders' hands when diamonds are 5-2. The defense will continue diamonds, South winning the ♦A.

If either defender has 4 trumps including the ♠Q, it will be necessary to use the ♠10 to force out the ♠Q. South should lead a low spade out of his hand. West will win the ♠Q, but South can easily draw trump and take the balance.

If South had won the ♦A on the first round of the suit, he would fail. After winning the ♠Q, West would play his other diamond to East. A diamond return from East would promote a second trump trick for West.

The recommended line of play will fail when East has a singleton ♠Q and 5 diamonds. After winning the ♠Q a third round of diamonds will promote a second trump trick. If East has a singleton spade, however, it is 4 times more likely that his singleton is a small card than it is the ♠Q.

notes: West leads the ♥K against 4♠. West cashes 2 top hearts and leads a third round, East ruffing. East's diamond return is won by South with the ♦A. It seems that the contract depends on the club finesse working.

West is almost certain to have the ♦K. West's takeout double makes it very likely that he has that card. As a further inference, if East had the ♦K he would probably have switched to a trump instead of a diamond away from the ♦K.

Assuming West has the ♦K, South can make the contract without finessing in clubs by running his winners. On the lead of the ♥Q West will be forced to come down to 2 clubs. The ♣Q will drop under the ♣A and ♣K.

The advantage of playing this way is that the contract will make when East has a doubleton ♣Q. On the ♥Q, West will have to come down to 2 clubs. South will know that the club finesse cannot gain. The ♣A and ♣K will drop East's doubleton ♣Q.

The above position is known as a show up squeeze. A show up squeeze will make a finesse unnecessary and will allow declarer to have an extra chance of dropping an offside honour when the finesse was losing.

notes: West leads the ♠Q against 3NT. West's spade opening lead should be won by South. A heart shift from West, attacking dummy's entry, would not be welcome. If South can develop the diamonds, he will be home.

The danger case is when one of the defenders has length in diamonds including the ♦A and ♦K. When South leads the ♦2, West must duck to shut out the diamonds. South must take this opportunity to win the trick in dummy. When East follows low, South has a second dummy entry to finesse twice in clubs.
If East has a singleton diamond honour he will win at trick 2. The contract will still have a chance as South can lead towards North's diamond holding, thus playing the suit for 2 losers.

On the given lie of the diamonds, South can also succeed by playing the ♦J to the ♦Q. This play is inferior as East, holding 3 diamonds to the ♦A and ♦K, will be able to win and prevent South from getting any diamond tricks. The contract will have no chance, regardless of what happens in clubs.

If East has this diamond holding, he will win the play of the ♦2 to the ♦10. South can hold up once in spades, and force East to duck the ♦J. South can now get 3 club tricks if East has 3 or fewer clubs headed by the ♣K. He crosses in hearts, takes a club finesse, cashes the ♣A, and surrenders a club trick to the ♣K. South can discard his spade loser when East cashes the ♦A and win the last 3 tricks.

notes: West leads the ♠K against 3NT. South should duck West's spade opening lead. When West continues spades it is safe to win the ♠A as East is marked with only 2 spades by West's weak 2 bid.

Only 4 club tricks are needed to make the contract. It may seem that South should guard against West having a singleton ♣K by playing the ♣A on the first round. Leading the ♣A play will not work when East has a singleton ♣K as West will have a certain club entry to cash his spades.

To guard against both possibilities, South should lead the first round of clubs from the dummy. South crosses to the dummy and leads a club. If East plays the ♣K, South ducks and the contract is safe.

If East follows low, South plays the ♣A, dropping the ♣K if it is singleton. If West follows low, South can return to the dummy and play clubs towards the closed hand. Notice that ducking the second round of spades will give East a chance to discard a singleton ♣K on the third round of spades. West will have a certain entry and the contract will be defeated.

notes: West leads the ♥K against 7♠. West's opening lead marks him with the ♥Q. South wins the ♥A, draws trump, and finds himself a trick short. It looks like South will need either 3-3 clubs or the diamond finesse to work.

If East has the ♦K, the contract is certain without taking the diamond finesse. South can cash the ♦A and run the spades. If West began with club length, he will be squeezed on the last spade. West must part with the ♥Q, establishing South's ♥J, or discard a club, making North's clubs good.
If East started with club length along with the ♦K, he will be forced to set up either South's ♦Q or North's fourth club when the last trump is cashed.

If the diamond finesse was losing, South's only hope is that West also has length in clubs. West will be squeezed in 3 suits on the run of the spades. Due to the presence of a third threat suit against West, West is squeezed on the second last spade. Anything West discards will give up a trick.
The diamond finesse can never gain over the squeeze approach. If the cards are distributed as above, South must play for a squeeze.

It is not necessary to cash the ♦A early. In this ending, if West had the ♦K he would have had to discard it already. When East has the ♦K, the ♦A will squeeze West in hearts and clubs as before. South can also succeed by cashing North's top clubs. When West shows up with a club stopper, the diamond finesse can be taken with complete confidence. West's last 2 cards are known to be the ♥Q and a club.

notes: West leads the ♦10 against 6♠. East wins the ♦A and returns the suit. South's only possible loser is in the trump suit.

South must play to prepare for a possible trump coup against 4 spades to the ♠J in East's hand. Before drawing trump, South should cash the ♣A and play another club, ruffing in hand. To draw trump, South should start by cashing the ♠A or ♠Q on the first round of the suit. On the second round of trump, West discards. North wins the ♠K and another club is ruffed.

South's trump length has been reduced to that of East's. For the trump coup to work, East must have 3 or more hearts. There is no need to cash South's last diamond which would risk East having a doubleton diamond.

South cashes 3 rounds of hearts, overtaking with the ♥A on the third round. North's fourth heart is played. East must follow (it would make no difference if he could ruff) and South discards his good diamond.
At trick 12, South is essentially in a position to finesse against the ♠J despite the fact that North has long been out of spades.

notes: West leads the ♦K against 6♥. The only possible problem is a 4-1 trump break. In that case, South must try to establish the dummy, ruffing 2 of North's diamonds and discarding North's remaining diamond and club losers on South's spades.
West's diamond lead should be ducked in the dummy and ruffed by South. The ♥A and ♥Q are cashed. When West discards on the second round of trump, South must play carefully.

South crosses in spades and leads another diamond, ruffing in the closed hand. South tries to cross again in spades. East cannot afford to ruff as the North and South hands still have a link in spades.

When East discards, the ♥K can be cashed. A heart trick is conceded to East. North's ♦A and ♣A can handle any return East makes. South will be able to run his spades without any worry of East ruffing in.

notes: West leads the ♦9 against 6NT. If West wins the ♦A and returns the suit South will make the contract despite the fact that both spades and hearts are not breaking as long as one defender has length in both suits.

On the last round of clubs, West, holding length in both spades and hearts, will be squeezed. A spade discard will establish a trick for South's fourth spade. A heart discard will allow North's hearts to run.

East can make South's task more difficult by ducking the ♦A at trick 1. East has essentially refused to rectify South's loser count down to 1. A simple squeeze can no longer function. A 2 loser squeeze, known as a stepping stone squeeze, can be executed to make the contract.

To clarify the position (although this is not necessary), South can cash 2 rounds of hearts and 3 rounds of spades. On the last club, West must keep both of his hearts and a spade guard. West is thus forced to part with his low diamond, his link to East's ♦A.

South can now cash his remaining heart honour and exit a spade. West wins the spade trick, but he must lead a heart to North's ♥A at trick 13. The stepping stone squeeze is a 2 loser, 3 suit squeeze that can be used to enable declarer to take tricks that would normally not be available due to a blocked suit.

notes: West leads the ♥J against 6NT. West's heart lead marks him with the ♥10. South is a trick short. If East wins the ♥A, South will be able to squeeze West in the majors if West began with 4 or more spades.
This will be the end position. On South's last club, West has no answer. A heart discard will establish North's ♥9. A spade discard will make North's third spade high.
East defends well by ducking the opening lead. East has effectively refused to rectify the count for South. A 2 loser squeeze, known as a vise, may still succeed when West has 4 or more spades.

On the last round of clubs West must guard the spades. West must discard a heart and North's small spade is discarded. West is now down to a singleton ♥10. South leads his remaining heart honour, establishing a trick with dummy's ♥9.

notes: West leads the ♣K against 4♥. The defense takes 2 club tricks and the third round is ruffed by East. South wins the spade shift and draws trump.

South now has a complete count on the hand. East started with 6 spades (for his weak 2 bid), 2 hearts, and 2 clubs. East must have exactly 3 diamonds. The ♦Q will not drop under the ♦A and ♦K, meaning South has a sure diamond loser.
If East started with the ♦Q he can be trump squeezed. South leads out all but 1 of his hearts. On South's second last heart, a diamond is thrown from dummy and East is squeezed.

A diamond discard will make the ♦Q drop under the ♦A and ♦K. South has a trump remaining to cross to his hand and enjoy the ♦J. A spade discard will allow South to cross to the dummy and establish a spade trick by ruffing. Dummy has a diamond entry to cash the good spade.

The simple trump squeeze matures with 1 loser. A defender is squeezed in 2 suits, 1 of which can be established by ruffing if the defender pitches from that suit. The other suit will become blocked at the time of the squeeze. The hand opposite the trump must have at least 2 entries. This type of squeeze is automatic, succeeding against either defender.
